 In 2008, Heath Ledger’s daughter inherited his estate, valued in reports at $16.3M to $20M; his 2003 will, signed before her birth, left her out
 In 2008, reports said Heath Ledger’s daughter Matilda would inherit his estate, over $16.3M, though his 2003 will left her out. His family chose to gift it.
 Published on: Oct 24, 2026, 11:16:29 IST By HT US Desk Prefer HT on Google Share via 
 Copy link 
 Think about who would get your things if something happened to you tomorrow. Many people in their twenties have no clear answer, and a lot of people who do write a will treat it like a box ticked and forgotten. The Associated Press reported in 2008 that actor Heath Ledger signed a will on April 12, 2003, leaving everything to his parents and three sisters. His daughter was not yet born, and the will never caught up with his life. What followed shows the value of an old piece of paper. 
 Heath Ledger’s will did not name his daughter, Matilda, who was born two years after he signed it. (Shutterstock) A will signed before Matilda was born 
 Ledger signed the will about two and a half years before his daughter, Matilda Rose, was born on October 28, 2005, to Ledger and actress Michelle Williams. The document listed assets and cash of just $118,000. Ledger died of an accidental prescription drug overdose in his Manhattan apartment in New York City on January 22, 2008, at age 28. The will had not been changed after Matilda’s birth, and she was not named in it.
 How the estate reached Matilda 
 In late September 2008, the AP reported, citing Australia’s Sunday Times, that two-year-old Matilda would inherit all of her father’s estate. There had been suggestions that Williams might make a claim on behalf of her daughter. Ledger’s father, Kim, told the paper there was no claim, saying, “Our family has gifted everything to Matilda.” The estate was thought to be worth over $16.3 million, the paper said, well in excess of the $118,000 in the will, though it was unclear whether that estimate included an expected life insurance payout. But Mark Dyson, an Adelaide accountant and one of the executors of the estate, could not reveal Matilda’s share. These accounts point to a family decision rather than a court order or legal fight.
 Ledger's family later gave Matilda his estate, avoiding a reported court dispute. (Wikimedia Commons) What the law says about a child left out 
 Family provision laws differ across Australian states. Ledger was born in Perth, so Western Australia’s law is used here only as an example, and the reports did not say which state’s law would have applied or that any claim was filed. Under the Inheritance (Family and Dependants Provision) Act 1972 , as it stood in 2008, a child of the deceased alive at the time of death could apply to the Supreme Court. If the court found that the will did not make adequate provision for proper maintenance, support, education, or advancement in life, it could order a lump sum or regular payments. Applications had to be made within six months of the administrator becoming entitled to administer the estate, although a court could allow a late application. The act was later amended and renamed the Family Provision Act 1972, so these points describe the law at the time of Ledger’s death. Even so, they show that a will leaving out a child is not necessarily the last word. 
 Why some experts push back 
 Not everyone believes courts should intervene often in these cases. Anthony Gray, in a 2017 paper in the Australian Law Journal , “Family Provision Application: A Critique,” examined recent cases in which wills had been successfully challenged for failing to provide adequately for family members. The paper argues that courts have been too quick to interfere with a person's choices concerning their own property and that this power should be used only exceptionally. That view captures the tension at the heart of these arguments. A will merely reflects the wishes of one person. There are family provision laws to protect close relatives. In the case of Ledger, the family decided to give everything to Matilda, so no court had to consider those ideas.
 A simple lesson for young adults 
 A will is a snapshot of one moment, and life can change quickly. An old will does not adjust itself to a new baby, a marriage, or a move. Matilda, now 20, inherited the estate because her family was generous, not because the law compelled her to. Every family is different, so it is important to review your will after major life events. It takes little time, and it can spare loved ones from guessing what you wanted.
